evidence_ledger.rationale: The paragraph index identifies CLOSPEN3's 1000-MAIN and 2000-PEN paragraphs, locating the computation and its caller for this case.

2000-PEN derives a breach day from calendar elapsed days and working days, then calculates WS-DELAY-CAL-DAYS and multiplies it by 500; this is the direct computation to compare with the clause's calendar-day basis.

The >= 7 condition enters the calculation at the seven-working-day edge, so it is a boundary candidate; the later counterexample supports the selected D3 because it shows a wrong penalty amount for calendar-day delay.
1000-MAIN accepts only calendar-days-elapsed and work-days-elapsed, performs 2000-PEN, and displays the computed penalty, showing the calculation is reachable on those inputs.
The scoped matches show the penalty computation uses 500 and show no 200 rate locus; the amount is not the stale 200 value.
The declarations distinguish WS-CAL-DAYS-ELAPSED from WS-WORK-DAYS-ELAPSED and define WS-DELAY-CAL-DAYS, while the calculation derives the latter through the working-day count.

The penalty slice connects both accepted elapsed counts to a breach-day calculation using WS-WORK-DAYS-ELAPSED - 7, then computes the penalty from WS-DELAY-CAL-DAYS; algebraically the resulting delay count is working days beyond seven.

A run_cobol reproduction of the observed 2000-PEN arithmetic with 12 calendar days and 8 working days prints PENALTY: 000050000, showing the formula counts one day although a Monday request followed by seven working days through Friday and closure Monday spans three calendar days after the deadline.

response.thought: The reachable penalty computation uses working days beyond the seven-day window as the number of calendar delay days. A case with a Friday deadline and Monday closure is undercounted.

prediction.rationale: In 2000-PEN, the source derives WS-SLA-BREACH-DAY by subtracting (WS-WORK-DAYS-ELAPSED - 7) from calendar elapsed days, then subtracts that result from calendar elapsed days to obtain WS-DELAY-CAL-DAYS. The calendar-day terms cancel, leaving working days beyond seven. Multiplying that count by 500 undercounts the clause's per-calendar-day penalty when the delay crosses a weekend: for a Monday request, the seventh working day is Friday and Monday closure is three calendar days late, but 12 elapsed calendar days and 8 working days produce only 500.

response.claim: Commercial banks must honour closure requests within at most 7 working days, subject to dues; failure incurs a penalty of at least Rs 500 for each calendar day of delay until closure, provided no outstanding.

exec_probe.description: For a Monday request with the seventh working day on Friday and closure Monday, 12 calendar days and 8 working days represent three calendar days of delay; the source output shows a one-day penalty.

response.final_answer: The calculation counts working days beyond the seven-day window as calendar delay days, so it undercounts the penalty when the delay crosses a weekend.
